>Sorry, the poster has you nailed to a board (something that might happen in a

>languish in abandonment because of *the bottom line*.

DANCY:I will point out that both of those games were inactive long before
WotC acquired FRPG, and that I had absolutely nothing to do with
stopping development of them. They were "dead" then, and they're
"dead" now, and there are complex market forces at work that will keep
them "dead" for some time longer, no matter how much you want the
situation to be otherwise. I can make the games, and I can market the
games, and I can support the games, but I don't sell the games. And

VtES.

> You have never denied it.

DANCY:I am actively trying to determine if there is a case to be made for
printing Silent Impact. If I can do so on a break-even basis (surely
even you won't begrudge me the right to not lose money on a game),
we'll print it.

> You could care less if they are much better games.

DANCY:I do not think that either product is a better game than the products
we have in production currently, or planned for release in the future.
Both games are now more than two years behind the development curve,
and both suffer from serious gameplay flaws, unbalanced cards,
problems with rules and other severe difficulties that would require
substantial revision before I'd be willing to move forward. Both
games, while cricitcally acclaimed are far below my minimum standards
for game play and for quality of gaming experience.

We're experimenting with that type of revision right now. You're
about to see the results when Rage ships next month (you can see a
preview right now if you want - I'd be happy to stick a Rage preview
deck in with that Doomtown deck....). We spent nearly two years
killing ourselves trying to update a TCG. We don't have any idea if
it can be done successfuly yet. Ask me in a year if the effort was
worth it.

I commented on this in rec.games.trading-cards.misc. Shortly put, I
strongly disagree with you assessment of Vampire as being "behind the
development curve". L5R, which is a not-bad game, has still *less*
innovative features as compared to Magic than Vampire. The storyline
approach has merit, but otherwise it's basically a glorified Magic
clone. Is that your idea of a state-of-the-art game?

> Correct me if I'm mistaken, but hasn't there been about 100+ messages
> in the past couple of weeks about this exact situation in Jyhad/VtES
> on this group?

I'm not sure what you're commenting about on with that (seems you're
commenting on your own comment ;), but...

Yes, there has been a *lot* of discussion about the rules here
recently, because of LSJ's rule errata to fix some stupid earlier
Rules Team rulings and the few obviously overpowered cards in the
game.

Frankly, I would have been surprised if there hadn't been heated
discussion. This game is played by a lot of people and has a
long-established player base, all change always meets resistance ;)

> What do you all think about the current state of the Jyhad/VtES rules
> and card base?

Rules
-----

A new edition of the rules would be great (i.e. the old rules with the
new LSJ rulings added). I believe that LSJ is working on something
like this.

Otherwise, I think the current Vampire rules are fine, and the basic
rules work very well both in a casual and a tournament setting. I love
the fact that the game is balanced enough not to require a wildly
different set of tournament rules, or a "banned from tournament play
because of power" list of cards. Very few games can say the same.

Having recently taught five new people to play, I find that the new
rules are quite easily taught to newbies. The only thing causing
confusion is the various older versions of errataed cards, and the
ambiguous wordings on especially the older (Jyhad) cards. More on this
below.

Cards
-----

I would *really* like to see a 2nd edition, using the same card art
but correcting the card texts to match current errata. It would
immeasurably help new players, and older players would like it as well
-- there has been discussion about this in this newsgroup. Yes, I
would personally buy boxloads of a 2nd edition, even though I already
have all the Jyhad/Vampire cards. Having correct and unambiguous card
texts would be fantastic.

There are also the few severely erratad problem cards from the
expansions, including reprints of them in a hyphotetical 2nd edition
would gain great favor from players, I suspect.

The current card base is usable (i.e. the game can continue to grow in
popularity with what exists), but a new expansion would give a huge
boost. Especially the Sabbat clans are greatly hampered right now, an
expansion with more Sabbat vampires would go to great lengths to fix
this... and since the Sabbat expansion sold so well, I doubt that such
an expansion would be a financial flop. I know for a fact that the
players over here would line up to buy such a thing.

Mr. Dancey, despite my having said some perhaps harsh words about the
percieved lack of FRPG support for Vampire before, I really appreciate
the effort you put into being online and communicating with us. I
don't agree with many of your views, but I hope that we can pursuade you
and your company that supporting Vampire is viable. I think it is, and
I have hands-on experience with the fact that that if anything, the
game is gaining players. If FRPG would put even a part of the effort
they put into supporting L5R into support for Vampire, the game would
flourish (with the side effect of turning an exisiting and time-proven
product into cash for WotC, which is naturally FRPG's goal in this
exercise).

//Petri

Messages.Author: Alan Flesch
Messages.Body:
> What do you all think about the current state of the Jyhad/VtES rules
> and card base?

Current state of Jyhad/VtES rules :

The major problem with the rules set is the complex of rules,
errata, and addenda (for lack of anything else to call it)
which were grafted onto the rules set by the Rules Team.
In the earliest days, with only one card set, the rules set
was explained and some minor shifts in rules occurred
(I was going through an old Duellist last night when the
D Bleed issue was being put forward for vote ie. should
D Bleeds be omni-directional?)

The shift from Jyhad to V:tES caused some problems in the
rules set as cards were 're-worded' to fit a template. The card
templates changed as fundamental sections of the rulebook
were re-evaluated (omni-directional D-Bleeds, eg.) LSJ ,
in his earliest days, compiled the errata and the rulings
together (much as Jeff Alexander does for L5R - a volunteer
archivist).

It became increasingly clear that the Rules Team was out of
touch with the game itself, and was relying largely on rules-
lawyering (rather than playtesting) to resolve disputes.
Templates were re-written, and cards were issued errata to
fit into these revised templates. The players' guide which
was printed contained many inaccuracies and omissions,
obvious to anyone with a casual knowledge of Jyhad's
operations.

With the expansions, the newest templates were followed;
this caused problems if the fundamental rule changed, causing
the templates to be no longer functional. (eg. weapons going
from 1 hand damage to +1 hand damage to strike:+1 hand
damage - this gave rise to large convoluted explanations that
weapons were not hand strikes but based on basic hand damage
of the acting minion... etc.)

The current crisis is based on the efforts of LSJ to bring
consistency to the rules set and balance to the game. (Read
that as neutral; I have an opinion, but I am also trying
to be fair to the opposing opinion) LSJ has an immense
knowledge of how the rules/errata/explanations work;
however, the wordings of the rules and the way that the
rules have operated in the past have caused diverging
opinions on how the errata _ought_ to be interpreted/
understood.

Current state of Jyhad/V:tES cardbase :

The initial print run of Jyhad was, in most opinions, and
incredibly balanced and well-conceived set. A multitude of
varying play styles and deck strategies were possible.
The balance was such that observable changes in deck
construction were visible : the metagame was a real and
almost predictable element of Jyhad play.

V:tES was printed with abundant supplies of Jyhad
still in-print. The first of the 'abusive' cards was printed,
Archon Investigation, indicating a power escalation
within the game. The first expansion, Dark Sovereigns,
received only a lukewarm reception; the second, Ancient
Hearts, was more avidly sought (largely because of the
presence of two broken cards : Return to Innocence and
the Tomb of Raamses III. As I recall, Dog Packs were also
quite prized at the time...

The problem with the two expansions here was the conscious
decision of Wizards not to print many vamps in them, nor to
make their disciplines as robust as the original ones. The
Followers of Set are underpowered and designed in such a way
that their 3 in-clan disciplines are only on the largest vampires.
The Giovanni received some interesting cards without really
making Necromancy a viable discipline.

Sabbat re-introduced the set (trying to do for Vampire what
Ice Age did for Magic ). taking into consideration 4CL individuals
by re-introducing cards with effects similar to ones in the first
set but with new names. Unfortunately, it also introduced a
counterspell card, Direct Intervention, which became the standard
'excuse' for any card in the game.

It is no coincidence that, of the top 5 cards considered 'broken'
that 4 come from expansions. The sets were engineered with a
'power escalation' model which made the game increasingly
reliant on having one of these 'power cards'.

My opinions
-------------------

I see no overwhelming reason not to create a new expansion. There
would be several predicates before such an expansion would be
viable :

1) The distributors would need to be convinced that a demand exists.
I subscribe to the Ars Magica listserv, and John Nephew, the
president of Atlas Games, regularly comments on the state of the
industry, and explains the status of products (so to speak). Your
comments on distributor's reluctance to carry 'inert' product echoes
what Mr. Nephew says : distributors don't take chances on anything
anymore. Atlas games has a warehouse full of On the Edge cards,
Ars Magica and Over the Edge sourcebooks, etc., all of which his
distributors insist is 'out of print'. Not because of misinformation,
but because they don't _want_ to carry it.

2) The market needs to be acknowledged for its real size and
enthusiasm. This goes both ways : the end-users need to accurately
evaluate how big the demand is; contrariwise, the producer needs
to acknowledge and support the product itself in an attempt to
'create' a new market. After all, L5R had _no_ market initially --
it's not based on a licence, it had no backstory, no word-of-mouth,
nothing but a dream and a hope. A market was _created_ for
L5R, and there is nothing to say that a similar thing couldn't happen
with V:tES.

3) The rules need to be adequately revised and a new rulebook issued.
A single, standardized rulebook with examples should be issued,
taking into account all templates and rules clarifications. To quote
your message :

Both games are now more than two years behind the development curve,
and both suffer from serious gameplay flaws, unbalanced cards,
problems with rules and other severe difficulties that would require
substantial revision before I'd be willing to move forward.

A single standardized rulebook could address these issues. I differ
in my opinion that Vampire suffers from 'serious gameplay flaws';
the only questionable areas of rules regarded paralyzation and
aggrivated damage. Aggrivated damage has been returned to its
original state (before it was 'revised' by the Rules Team) and
Paralyzation has been removed from the rules set.

4) The game has to change to a 'player-friendly' format. The history
of V:tES players to its producers has not been happy. It is an
unfortunate fact that Jyhad was created in the post-Magic boom
that saw dozens of games created only to die out. Jyhad has survived
that boom (largely because it was coupled to Magic through WotC,
and so would be retained rather than written off as a bankruptcy
loss). Jyhad was overproduced, then kept alive through a series
of ill-advised and poorly handled expansions. The Rules Team
waffled on rulings, the net-reps didn't interact with the list (largely
because of their competing duties re: Magic) and poor business
decisions were made regarding card-backs. Much of the hostility from
the V:tES players is 'backseat' phenomena - we were an afterthought
to the success of Magic. Player-interaction (on the model of L5R's
Imerial Assembly) may do much to bring the feud to a close.

5) My very own humble opinion : There is absolutely no reason
why Vampire could not be brought into a Storyline/Clan War
format. Long ago, you remarked that Netrunner failed because
of its 'abstractness' - it couldn't be lodged into an 'identity' modality
where the player of the deck could enter into the storyline of
the game. V:tES is suited to doing so, having well-defined Clans
and tactics associated with each clan. Clans such as the Malkavians
and the Setites would benefit from such specificity, gaining in
character what they have lacked hitherto in gameplay. As you have
noted, storyline increases player interest, as they begin to feel that
they are involved with the future of the playset. As people have noted,
Jyhad is a much more interesting game than Rage (I have large collections
of both, but it is Jyhad that I play most often), and has greater
depth-of-play.

I'm emailing this as well as posting it, to ensure that everyone gets a
look at my ideas. :) (I'm arrogant that way, I guess...)

Alan (aj)

That, sir, is >exactly< my analysis of the game as it stands
presently. Well done.

I'll add to your analysis the concern that one of the biggest issues
that WotC has looked at for a very long time is the issue of
competitive play.

We know (as well as any such thing can be said to be "known") that
regular, organized competitive play is what drives the TCG market for
expansion product. Basic Sets can sell on their merits, but
expansions require an active metagame and a viable source of quality
opponents in order to generate sales.

I have had long talks with the DCI and with other people who have
played VtES in a competitive environment, and everyone I have spoken
to acknowledges (if not agrees to) two salient points:

1) The game virtually requires 4 people to function effectively
2) The games are more often determined by an opponent's >mistake<
rather than your superior play.

Point 2 may very well be an artifiact of Point 1 - the cumulative
errors introduced during play are multiplied by the number of people
at the table. But what Point 2 says is: Winning a competitive VtES
event is more determined by luck than by skill.

To find a way out of that mess, the DCI has looked at several schemes
for "point scoring" that would be less influenced by the people in the
game not being as effective as they should be objectively. They have
yet to find a viable solution.

While that condition lingers, the organized play component of the VtES
brand will suffer greatly from people feeling that victory is
capricious and luck-based - very unappealing to today's sophisticated
regular TCG players.

> errors introduced during play are multiplied by the number of people

> event is more determined by luck than by skill.

How does this differ from, say, chess, bridge, or poker? Part of skill
is 'not making significant mistakes' in game play; most of the iterations
of a chess game are well-known and even named; it can be argued that
chess devolves into 'who knows the most iterations' and can steer
play into one inevitable result. Contract bridge depends on the skill
of your partner, and relying that your partner doesn't make any mistakes.
Poker, the most random of the games here mentioned, still requires a
tremendous amount of skill to play : each individual hand of poker
dealt is randomly determined - but the superior poker player will
beat me over a set of games.

Each of these three games (chess, bridge, poker) has a significant
tournament following, despite significant 'gameplay' flaws re: luck.

CCG's have an aggrivated problem with luck with deck construction.
Deck construction is almost entirely skill based (an experienced
player can design tightly-focussed decks with defenses against
various possible counter-strategies). Also, an experienced player
can reasonably expect what kinds of decks will be present at an
active tournament scene. However, the pairing of individual decks
is always a matter of luck. You have very little control in arranging
who your opponants will be.

Returning to a point thrown out earlier : a significant part of skill is
the ability to recognize the failures of gameplay on the part of your
opponant and to exploit these failures. To recognize this isn't the
same thing as saying that 'the game is driven by luck'. It requires
a high degree of skill to recognize that a 'mistake' has been made
in many cases. You may even put under the category of skill the
ability to minimize luck.

and "non-honour" decks (those which don't try to gain honour, but aren't
really prepared to lose it either... a lot of Mantis decks fall into this
category, because they have few high-honour personalities). That deck will

miserably to a Shadowlands deck. A well-constructed Kaiu Crab honour-runner

dealing with dishonour, usually.

to resurrect my Crane deck and try it out in a tournament, the game would
basically be whether or not I draw to play against Scorpion. If so, I lose.

>How does this differ from, say, chess, bridge, or poker?

Perhaps you misunderstand me. In chess, there are no third party
players. In poker, the play can be influenced by third party players,
but it is normally very difficult for one player's "poor play" to
improve the play of another participant without improving the play of
all the participants in the game. I have no opinion on bridge - I've
not played enough (or recently enough) to formulate a comparative
argument.

Imagine a four player game of VtES, players named A, B, C and D. A
preys on B, B on C, etc.

The problem with the current way that competitive VtES is played is
that if Person B plays poorly, it benefits Person C (due to the fact
that you cannot normally attack anyone in the game - only the person
defined as your prey. So the disruptivly "bad" effects of B are all
directed solely at C. Please - let's leave voting and other general
type actions aside for the moment, this example is for illustrative
purposes only) So, even if players A and D are doing fine, player C
has a cumulative advantage over them, because the person who should be
affecting Player C in a negative way, Player B, is playing poorly.

So players A and D are in the unfortunate position of being "crippled"
in this game because they are not seated adjacent to poor player B.
Rather, I should say that player C is receiving an "unfair advantage"
by being lucky enough to be preyed on by Player B.

If a "swiss" system is used to determine matchups, the result is often
a situation where the winner goes undefeated. Because of the effect I
describe above, the putative "best player" in the event may lose a
game or two >through no fault of their own, or due to the luck of the
draw<, but because >another player< inadvertantly assisted a third
competitor to victory.

Please tell me that's not as confusing as it reads. :)

Messages.Body:
Ry...@frpg.com (Ryan S. Dancey) wrote:
> Imagine a four player game of VtES, players named A, B, C and D. A
> preys on B, B on C, etc.
>

> The problem with the current way that competitive VtES is played is
> that if Person B plays poorly, it benefits Person C (due to the fact
> that you cannot normally attack anyone in the game - only the person
> defined as your prey. So the disruptivly "bad" effects of B are all
> directed solely at C. Please - let's leave voting and other general
> type actions aside for the moment, this example is for illustrative
> purposes only) So, even if players A and D are doing fine, player C
> has a cumulative advantage over them, because the person who should be
> affecting Player C in a negative way, Player B, is playing poorly.

Yes, in our circle of play this dynamic is referred to as the "ineffectual
predator" syndrome. What typically happens is that player D recognizes
that player B is an ineffectual predator, and actively assists player A
to oust player B. If player D is playing a Rush Combat or a Vote deck,
such assistance can be direct. If player D has an Intercept Combat deck,
he "lets up" on player A and concentrates on intercepting player C. Prior
to the 7/7 RTR rulings, if player D had a bleed deck, he could cross table
bleed player B. Now, player D is pretty much stuck -- all he can do is
"let up" on player A and do nothing.

However, your comments ignore what I feel is the strongest point of VtES
as a multiplayer game: it avoids the "gang up on the leader" syndrome.
In games such as Shadowfist or Doomtown, when a player is identified as
"leading" then every other player in the game gangs up on that player to
stop him/her. What frequently happens is that the leader is weakened,
and then some other player threatens to win, is weakened, etc., etc., ad
nauseum. Eventually _all_ the players are within striking distance of
winning no matter what deck they're playing. In VtES, since you don't
care about the "leader" unless he/she is a near-term threat, this happens
much, much less frequently. Normally, your deck is only concerned with
predator and prey. This make VtES stand out in a positive way from all
other multi-player CCGs I've seen.
